docs.title: Home
docs.text:
pavvis is a Python package for analysing and visualising gene Presence/Absence Variation (PAV) data from pangenome studies.

pavvis was designed to be easy to use and optimised for large-scale genomic datasets. To get the best use out of this Python package, we recommend reading through our concepts page, that will help you to understand the data structures associated with all analysis in this Python package.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Getting started with pavvis.
from pavvis import PavMatrix
import pavvis.plots.presence as presence

pm = PavMatrix("pav_matrix.csv", "metadata.csv")
print(pm)
# PavMatrix(34295 genes × 1039 samples)

print(pm.gene_counts)
# {'core': 2, 'soft_core': 252, 'dispensable': 9853, 'private': 24186, 'absent': 2}

presence.frequency_histogram(pm).show()

docs.title: What is a PAV matrix?
docs.text:
A Presence/Absence variation (PAV) matrix is a binary matrix commonly used in pangenome analysis to represent whether a gene is present (1) or absent (0) across a population, often across thousands of genes.

This information can be stored in a number of different ways; however, pavvis standardises the input data structures based on the following format:

A gene PAV matrix in pavvis can be loaded from a CSV file with the following format:

sample_a sample_b sample_c gene_alpha 1 0 1 gene_beta 1 1 1 gene_gamma 0 0 1
  • Rows — gene identifiers (must be unique). These can be any stable identifier: UniProt IDs, structural annotation IDs, nucleotide sequences, or custom labels.
  • Columns — sample/accession identifiers (must be unique).
  • Values — strictly 0 (absent) or 1 (present).

docs.title: PAV and associations with sample metadata
docs.text:
pavvis is designed to integrate gene PAV analysis with sample level metadata. To do this, pavvis requires the user to supply a separate metadata.csv. This enables plots and summary statistics to be generated for both discrete and continuous variables.

In this context, common sample metadata may include columns such as population_group, ancestral_group, or longitude/latitude.

docs.title: The metadata.csv file
docs.text:
A separate metadata CSV file provides sample-level annotations (e.g. species, country of origin, growth habit). Its row index must match the PAV matrix column headers exactly.

For example, a valid metadata CSV for the matrix above:

population_group climate longitude latitude sample_a GroupA Temperate -0.27 51.49 sample_b GroupB Tropical -99.13 19.42 sample_c GroupA Temperate 4.90 52.37

The metadata CSV may contain any number of columns with any mix of discrete or continuous values.

docs.title: Gene categories
docs.text:
Pangenomic studies often define gene sets based on their presence or absence across the whole population. pavvis classifies every gene into one of three categories based on its presence pattern across all samples in the matrix:

Category Definition Core Present in every sample (1 across the entire row) Variable Present in at least one but not all samples Absent Absent from every sample (0 across the entire row)

docs.title: Variable genes
docs.text:
In PAV analysis, variable genes tend to be of the most interest to researchers. pavvis classifies variable genes in a PAV matrix as one of three subcategories to add more depth to matrix analysis. These values are based on the relative frequency of each genes presence across the entire gene row in the pav matrix. The default values for these three subcategories are shown below:

Variable gene subclass Default presence frequency Soft Core >= 0.95 and < 1 Dispensable >= 0.15 and < 0.95 Private > 0 and < 0.15

Customising thresholds

These defaults are based on common thresholds used throughout pangenomic research papers. Depending on the number of samples in the PAV matrix, these thresholds may not be optimal — they can be overwritten when instantiating a new PavMatrix() object as shown below:

Building a PavMatrix object with custom variable gene thresholds
from pavvis.pav_matrix import PavMatrix

pm = PavMatrix(matrix_path="./pav.csv", 
              metadata_path="./metadata.csv",
              soft_core_min=0.90,
              dispensable_min=0.20,
              private_min=0.05)

print(pm.thresholds)

docs.title: Absent and core genes
docs.text:
In addition to variable genes, pavvis also defines two other types of gene:

  • absent genes are always defined as all 0 across the PAV matrix.
  • core genes are always defined as all 1 across the PAV matrix.

The default value for these gene categories cannot be changed.

docs.title: Exclusive genes
docs.text:
An exclusive gene is defined as a variable gene that is present in at least one sample belonging to a specific group whilst bieng completely absent from every sample outside that group. Exclusivity is always defined relative to a discrete metadata column (e.g. species, population, treatment).

For a gene to be classified as exclusive to group G:

  1. It must be present (1) in at least one sample where metadata[column] == G.
  2. It must be absent (0) in every sample where metadata[column] != G.

Core and absent genes are excluded from this analysis by definition — a core gene is present in all samples and therefore cannot be exclusive to any group, and an absent gene is present in no samples.

Exclusive genes are biologically interesting because they represent gene content that is unique to a particular group — for example, genes found only in a specific species, geographic population. A high exclusive gene count within a group may indicate lineage-specific gene content relating to processes such as adaption to local environments.

docs.title: Why handle PAV matrices as Python class objects?
docs.text:
pavvis represents a PAV matrix as a PavMatrix Python class rather than a loose collection of functions. This allows the object to:

  • Validate on load — bad inputs are caught immediately, not silently propagated.
  • Cache derived values — computationally expensive results (i.e. UMAP embeddings, pangenome curves, calculated jaccard distances) can be stored on the object after the first calculation and utilised by multiple different plotting functions.
  • Carry context — the PAV data and its metadata always travel together, reducing the chance of mismatched inputs in multistep workflows.

Example data

Throughout this documentation, we provide example data and plots that will allow users to visualise the outputs of the functions they are calling. This is particularly useful for the plotting subpackage, allowing users to see plots rendered for each function, as well as the input parameter values used. For generating these plots, we use a PAV matrix of variable genes that was generated as an outcome of the Watkins Wheat Pangenome in one of our previous research projects. The metadata file associated with all Watkins wheat samples is derived from research published by Cheng et al. (2024).

docs.title: Loading your data
docs.text:
pavvis requires two CSV files to generate a PavMatrix object. The PavMatrix class is central to the pavvis workflow.:

  • PAV matrix — genes as rows, samples as columns, values must be 0 or 1, i.e a binary matrix.
  • Metadata — samples as rows, any number of metadata columns
Building a PavMatrix object
from pavvis import PavMatrix

pm = PavMatrix(
    matrix_path="path/to/pav_matrix.csv",
    metadata_path="path/to/metadata.csv",
)

print(pm)
# PavMatrix(34295 genes × 1039 samples)

File formats

For examples of how these files should be formatted, see the concepts page.

When building the PavMatrix() class, pavvis will automatically validate that:

  • Both files exist on the system
  • Sample IDs of the PAV matrix columns match the metadata row indexes
  • All PAV values are binary (0 or 1) with no blank cells

docs.title: Exploring your data
docs.text:
Now you have generated a PavMatrix object, you can explore basic summary statistics using the class attributes.

Explore a PavMatrix using basic class attributes
# Get gene category counts
print(pm.gene_counts)
# {'core': 12, 'variable': 28761, 'absent': 5522}

# List gene IDs by category
print(pm.core_genes[:3])
print(pm.variable_genes[:3])
print(pm.absent_genes[:3])

# List exclusive variable genes for a metadata category
print(pm.exclusive_gene_counts("population_group"))
# {'GroupA': 183, 'GroupB': 204}

docs.title: First plot
docs.text:
Aside from allowing the user to easily group and summarise their data, the pavvis package also provides functions that allow the user to generate plots for thier data. All of these functions are contained in the plots module.

Build histograms to summarise gene presence in your PavMatrix
import pavvis.plots as pp

# Histogram of presence frequencies (log y-axis)
pp.presence_frequency_histogram(pm).show()

# Bar chart of top 50 genes by presence frequency
pp.presence_frequency_histogram(pm, type="bar").show()

docs.title: Subsetting
docs.text:
subset() returns a new PavMatrix restricted to selected samples and/or genes, so any analysis or plot can be rerun on part of the data — for example a single clade or region. Samples can be selected by ID, by a pandas query against the metadata, or both. The original object is never modified.

modern = pm.subset(query="clade == 'Modern'")
europe_deep = pm.subset(query="continent == 'Europe' and depth > 10")
pair = pm.subset(samples=["Ability", "Agron"], drop_absent=True)

print(modern)  # PavMatrix(34295 genes × 212 samples)

Gene categories are recomputed

Categories are always relative to the samples in the matrix. A gene that is variable across the full population may be core, or absent, within a subset. Use drop_absent=True to remove genes that no retained sample carries.

docs.title: subset
docs.text:
subset(samples=None, genes=None, query=None, drop_absent=False)

Return a new PavMatrix restricted to a subset of samples and/or genes.

Filters are combined: a sample is kept only if it is in samples (when given) and matches query (when given). Samples and genes keep their order from the original matrix. Gene categories are recomputed on the subset, so a gene that is variable across the full matrix may be core or absent within the subset. Thresholds are carried over; cached results (UMAP, Jaccard, PCoA) are not, and the original object is left unchanged.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default samples list[str] | None

Sample IDs to keep. Defaults to None (all samples).

None genes list[str] | None

docs.title: Summary tables
docs.text:
gene_table() and sample_table() collect per-gene and per-sample summaries into pandas DataFrames, ready to filter, sort, merge with other data (such as functional annotations), or export with .to_csv() as supplementary tables.

gt = pm.gene_table(column="clade")

gt.loc["gene_42"]                                  # everything about one gene
gt[gt.exclusive_to == "AG3"].index                 # genes found only in AG3
gt[(gt.category == "dispensable") & (gt.n_Modern == 0)]  # dispensable genes absent from Modern lines
gt.to_csv("gene_table.csv")

st = pm.sample_table(include_metadata=True)

st.sort_values("n_singletons", ascending=False).head(10)  # accessions carrying the most unique genes
st.groupby("clade")["n_private"].mean()                   # private gene content per clade
st["n_genes"].corr(st["depth"])                           # check gene counts against sequencing depth

Unclassified genes

By default private_min is 0, so every gene present in at least one sample gets a category. If you raise it (e.g. private_min=0.01), genes rarer than that threshold are no longer private, but they aren't absent either. gene_table() labels these genes "unclassified".

docs.title: UMAP
docs.text: Uniform Manifold Approximation Projection (UMAP) is a dimensionality reduction technique that is used to visualise high-dimensional data. In the context of PAV, it can help gain insight into the relationships between samples through similarity in PAV profiles. Generating UMAP embeddings can be done by calling the compute_umap() method. This is not automatically called on initial construction of new PavMatrix() objects, as it can be computationally intensive, particularly for large datasets.

docs.title: compute_umap
docs.text:
compute_umap(n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.1, metric='jaccard', random_state=None)

Compute a 3D UMAP embedding of the samples and cache it on this object.

Always computes 3 components so the result can be used for both 2D and 3D plots without recomputing. The embedding is computed on the transposed PAV matrix (samples × genes). Re-calling with the same parameters returns the cached result immediately. Re-calling with different parameters recomputes and overwrites the cache.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_neighbors int

UMAP n_neighbors parameter. Controls local vs global structure. Defaults to 15.

15 min_dist float

UMAP min_dist parameter. Controls how tightly points are packed. Defaults to 0.1.

0.1 metric str

Distance metric passed to UMAP. Defaults to 'jaccard', which ignores shared absences and is appropriate for binary PAV data.

'jaccard' random_state int | None

Random seed for reproducibility. Defaults to None.

None

Returns:

Type Description PavMatrix

self, so calls can be chained: pm.compute_umap().plot...

docs.title: PCoA
docs.text: Principal Coordinates Analysis (classical MDS) on Jaccard distance gives a linear ordination of the samples with a known proportion of variation per axis. compute_pcoa() caches the result for the PCoA plots.

docs.title: compute_pcoa
docs.text:
compute_pcoa(n_components=10)

Compute a PCoA (classical MDS) of the samples on Jaccard distance and cache it.

Distances are D = 1 − J, where J is the Jaccard similarity from compute_jaccard() (called automatically if needed). Jaccard distance is not Euclidean, so the decomposition yields some negative eigenvalues; only axes with positive eigenvalues are kept, and explained variance is each eigenvalue divided by the sum of all positive eigenvalues. Re-calling with the same n_components returns the cached result immediately.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_components int | None

Number of leading axes to keep. If fewer positive axes exist, all of them are kept. None keeps every positive axis. Defaults to 10.

10

Returns:

Type Description PavMatrix

self, so calls can be chained: pm.compute_pcoa().plot...

docs.title: Curve plots
docs.text: This submodule contains functions for building traditional pangenome curves and other line-plots for gaining insight into the variable gene profiles of a PAV matrix, including patterns that emerge from the accumulation of variable genes across groups defined in a metadata.csv file.

docs.title: Pangenome Curves
docs.text:
Pangenome curves allow researchers to assess the degree of 'completeness' for a pangenome. Pangenomes seek to capture all gene content shared across a population (all samples making up the the PAV matrix). A pangenome is made up of core gene content present in all samples, and variable gene content present in only a subset of samples.

A pangenome curve plots the accumulation of variable gene content as each genome is "added" to the PAV matrix. As more genomes are added, more of the variable material is captured, leading to a pattern of diminishing returns, where eventually, the addition of further genomes will add very little novel variable material.

docs.title: Traditional pangenome curve.
docs.text: A Traditional pangenome curve plots the accumulation of genomic content as each genome is added to the PAV matrix, curves quickly reaching a plateau infer that the pangenome for the species is relatively closed, and that a complete picture of all shared genomic content can be captured by a small number of samples. A curve that continues to rise without leveling off indicates that the pangenome is "open" for the population, and that the sample set has not captured a complete picture of the shared genomic content for the population.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Plots pangenome and core genome size curves on a shared y-axis as genomes are accumulated in random order. For each permutation a different sample ordering is drawn. At each step \(k\), the pangenome size is the count of genes with at least one presence (\(x_{g,i} = 1\)) across the first \(k\) samples; the core genome size is the count of genes present in all \(k\) samples. Both quantities are averaged over \(P\) random permutations, and the mean and ±1 standard deviation band are plotted for each curve. A pangenome curve that continues to rise steeply indicates an open pangenome; a core curve that decays quickly to near-zero confirms that gene content is highly variable across the population.

Performance

A high number of permutations can be computationally intensive for large PAV matrices. We recommend starting with a lower value (e.g. permutations=10) to verify the plot looks as expected, before increasing to a higher value for final figures.

For each permutation a random sample order is drawn. At each step k the pangenome size (union of all genes seen so far) and core size (intersection of all genes seen so far) are recorded. The mean and ±1 std band across permutations are plotted for both curves.

Interpretation

A pangenome curve that continues to rise without levelling off as more genomes are added indicates that the pangenome is open — additional sampling would likely reveal further novel gene content. A curve that plateaus early suggests a closed pangenome, where the gene repertoire of the population is well-captured by the existing sample set. Correspondingly, a core curve that falls steeply toward zero indicates that few genes are universally conserved across all samples, which is typical of species with highly variable accessory genomes.

docs.title: Variable gene accumulation curves.
docs.text:
A variable gene accumulation curve has no fundamental conceptual difference to a traditional pangenome curve, but seeks to plot the accumulation of variable gene content separate to the core genetic material. As the variable gene content increases with the addition of new genomes to the pangenome, the core genetic material decreases. This can be visualised as two distinct curves across the same plot, represented using 3-axis.

At each step \(k\), a random ordering of samples is drawn. The pangenome size is the count of genes present in at least one of the first \(k\) samples; the core size is the count of genes present in all \(k\) samples; and the variable gene count is the difference between the two. This is repeated across \(P\) random permutations, and the mean and ±1 standard deviation band are plotted for both curves.

Performance

A high number of permutations can be computationally intensive for large PAV matrices. We recommend starting with a lower value (e.g. permutations=10) to verify the plot looks as expected, before increasing to a higher value for final figures.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Plots core and variable gene counts on separate left/right y-axes as genomes are accumulated in random order. Each permutation draws a different sample ordering; the mean and ±1 std band across all permutations are shown. A steeply decaying core curve indicates an open pangenome; a flattening variable curve suggests the gene pool is near-saturated.

Mean and ±1 std bands across permutations are shown for both curves. Clicking a legend entry toggles its mean line and std band together.

A variable gene curve that presents a flat gradient indicates that the majority of the variable gene content has been captured for the population by the number of samples. In this case, the PAV matrix contains no core genes, so we expect the number of core genes to decrease quickly to near-zero as new variable material is added across the plot.

Adding genomes to the graph one group at a time may allow the researcher to identify groups that provide variable gene content not already captured in the shared material of previous groups and identify the existence of group-specific variable gene content.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Plots a separate accumulation curve for each group in a discrete metadata column. Unlike the grouped variable gene curve above, where groups are added one after another along a single curve, here each group's samples are accumulated independently and plotted on a shared axes starting from the first genome. This allows groups to be compared directly at equal sample sizes. The curve argument selects what is accumulated: the pangenome size (genes present in at least one of the first \(k\) samples), the core size (genes present in all \(k\) samples), or the variable gene count (the difference between the two). Within each group the sample order is randomly permuted \(P\) times, and the mean and ±1 standard deviation bands for each curve are shown. Groups with fewer than 2 samples are skipped with a warning.

Comparing groups of different sizes

Each group's curve ends at its own sample size. To compare groups fairly, read the curves at the same number of genomes — for example, at the size of the smallest group — rather than comparing their end points.

Performance

A high number of permutations can be computationally intensive for large PAV matrices. We recommend starting with a lower value (e.g. permutations=10) to verify the plot looks as expected, before increasing to a higher value for final figures.

docs.title: Jaccard Similarity Curves
docs.text:
The Jaccard similarity between two samples is the proportion of genes that are shared between them relative to the total number of genes present in either. Unlike simple overlap counts, it accounts for the size of each sample's gene set, making it a useful measure of overall genomic similarity. Because Jaccard similarity is calculated only over genes that are present in at least one sample, jaccard-distance does not take into account shared absence between samples.

Plotting mean pairwise Jaccard similarity as groups are added one at a time allows the researcher to assess how genomically distinct each group is from those already accumulated. A drop in similarity when a new group is introduced suggests that group carries a substantially different gene repertoire; a stable curve indicates the groups are broadly similar in their PAV profiles.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Plots mean pairwise Jaccard similarity across all accumulated genomes as groups are added in a fixed order. Within each group the sample order is randomly permuted P times whilst the group sequence itself is fixed. At each step \(k\), the mean Jaccard similarity is calculated across all pairs of the \(k\) genomes accumulated so far. The mean and ±1 standard deviation band across permutations are shown. A drop at a group boundary indicates the incoming group is divergent from those already accumulated; a stable curve indicates genomic similarity across groups.

Use case

This type of curve can be useful for assessing particular groups that may harbour interesting and novel variable genes, rare or absent across other groups, that may warrant further investigation.

Performance

A high number of permutations can be computationally intensive for large PAV matrices. We recommend starting with a lower value (e.g. permutations=10) to verify the plot looks as expected, before increasing to a higher value for final figures.

A drop when a new group is introduced indicates that group is divergent from those already seen; stability indicates similarity. The mean and ±1 std band across permutations are shown. docs.title: Heatmap plots
docs.text: This submodule contains functions for visualising the PAV matrix and the relationships between its samples and genes as heatmaps. Heatmaps provide a direct view of the underlying data that is complementary to association identification offered by the presence, curve, and variable gene submodules. They are particularly useful for identifying clustering structure, co-occurrence patterns, and the degree of genomic similarity across the sample set.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Renders the raw PAV matrix as a binary heatmap, with genes as rows and samples as columns. Each cell is coloured white (absent, 0) or navy (present, 1). Because large PAV matrices can contain tens of thousands of genes, the gene_set parameter (default 'variable') should be used to restrict the display to a biologically meaningful subset.

Heatmaps can be noisy, and we recommend first spending time filtering the PAV matrix to reduce genes and samples to increase the space available to render genes and samples of interest.

Planned functionality

We plan to extend pavvis with functions for automatic matrix filtering, such as pruning genes based on their degree of presence across the matrix, to make heatmap generation more streamlined for large datasets.

Sample columns can optionally be reordered by hierarchical clustering on Jaccard distance (col_cluster=True), which groups together samples with more similar PAV profiles. A colour-coded annotation strip can be added above the columns to label each sample by a discrete metadata variable, making it easy to assess whether clustering aligns with known biological groupings.

Prerequisites for clustering

col_cluster=True requires pm.compute_jaccard() to have been called first. See the PavMatrix API for details.

docs.text:
pav_heatmap(
    pm,
    gene_set="variable",
    col_cluster=False,
    color_by=None,
    show_gene_labels=False,
)

Each cell is coloured by absence (0) or presence (1). Genes are rows, samples are columns. An optional metadata annotation strip can be added above the heatmap to identify sample groups at a glance.

Samples that cluster together share similar variable gene content. When the annotation strip is visible, alignment between colour-coded groups and the clustering structure suggests that the metadata variable is a good predictor of PAV profile similarity. Isolated samples or samples that do not cluster with their group may contain unusual gene content worth investigating further.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Plots a symmetric sample × sample Jaccard similarity matrix as a heatmap. Each cell shows the pairwise Jaccard similarity between two samples, computed across all genes in the PAV matrix. Jaccard similarity accounts only for genes that are present in at least one of the two samples, ignoring shared absences.

Samples can be reordered by hierarchical clustering (cluster=True, the default) to group together the most similar samples. An optional annotation strip on both axes labels each sample by a discrete metadata column, making it straightforward to assess whether biological grouping corresponds to genomic similarity in the PAV matrix.

Prerequisites

This function requires pm.compute_jaccard() to have been called first. See the PavMatrix API for details.

docs.title: Indicator gene plots
docs.text: This submodule visualises the results of indicator_genes. The plot takes the results table as input, so the permutation test only has to be run once.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Shows the strongest indicator genes of each group as rows and the groups as columns. Each cell is the fraction of the group's samples that carry the gene. Colour strips on the left indicate each metadata group, The cell for a gene's own group is its fidelity (B); how pale the rest of the row is reflects its specificity (A).

docs.title: heatmap
docs.text:
heatmap(pm, indicators, column, top_n=10, q_max=0.05, show_gene_labels=True)

Plot the presence frequency of the top indicator genes in every group.

Rows are the strongest indicator genes of each group, columns are the groups, and each cell is the fraction of that group's samples carrying the gene. Genes are grouped by the group they indicate, so a good indicator shows as a dark cell in its own group's column and pale cells elsewhere. The cell in a gene's own group equals its fidelity B. A colour strip on the left marks each row's indicator group, using the same colours as the other group plots.

For each group, genes with q_value < q_max are ranked by stat (then by p_value and B to break ties) and the first top_n are shown. Groups with fewer significant genes show the ones they have.

from pavvis import PavMatrix
from pavvis.stats.indicator import indicator_genes
import pavvis.plots.indicator as indicator_plots

pm = PavMatrix("path/to/pav.csv", "path/to/metadata.csv")
res = indicator_genes(pm, "clade", permutations=999, random_state=0)

indicator_plots.heatmap(pm, res, "clade", top_n=5).show()

Interpretation

A row dark in its own column and white elsewhere is a gene restricted to that group and carried by most of its samples. A row that is dark in its own column but also dark in others indicates a gene enriched in, but not restricted to, the group. A row that is pale everywhere but darkest in its own column is a rare but group-specific gene. Gene IDs can be long; set show_gene_labels=False for a compact overview when gene IDs do not mean anything.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Plots the two components of the indicator value against each other for every significant indicator gene, with one panel per group. Specificity (A) is on the x-axis and fidelity (B) on the y-axis. Grey curves join points of equal IndVal.g statistic, so genes beyond the outer curve are the strongest indicators. Where the heatmap shows only the top genes, this plot shows all of them.

docs.title: PCoA plots
docs.text:
This submodule contains functions for visualising the Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA) of PAV matrices computed by pm.compute_pcoa(). PCoA (classical multidimensional scaling) places samples in a low-dimensional space so that the distances between them approximate their pairwise Jaccard distances (1 − Jaccard similarity), ignoring shared absences.

Unlike UMAP, PCoA is a linear, deterministic ordination, the proportion of variation in each group can be reported, and distances on the plot relate directly to the distance matrix used by PERMANOVA and dispersion tests.

Prerequisites

You must call pm.compute_pcoa() before using any function documented on this page. See the PavMatrix API for details. Jaccard distance is not Euclidean, so only axes with positive eigenvalues are kept, and explained variance is reported relative to the sum of the positive eigenvalues.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Plots two PCoA axes as a 2D scatter plot, with the percentage of variation explained in each axis title. Each point represents a sample. Colouring works the same way as the UMAP scatter plot.

Plot two PCoA axes of the samples as a 2D scatter plot.

Points represent samples. Axis titles show the percentage of variance each axis explains. Colouring behaves identically to pavvis.plots.umap.scatter: discrete columns produce a categorical legend; continuous columns use a Viridis colorscale.

required color_by str | None

An optional metadata column name to colour points by. Accepts both discrete and continuous columns. Defaults to None.

None components tuple[int, int]

The two 1-based PCoA axes to plot on x and y. Defaults to (1, 2).

(1, 2)

Type Description Figure

A Plotly Figure. Call .show() to display or .write_html() to export.

Raises:

from pavvis import PavMatrix
import pavvis.plots.pcoa as pcoa

    matrix_path="path/to/pav.csv",
    metadata_path="path/to/metadata.csv",

pm.compute_pcoa()
pcoa.scatter(pm, color_by="clade").show()
pcoa.scatter(pm, color_by="clade", components=(1, 3)).show()

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Plots samples on two PCoA axes with each group's centre (spatial median or mean) and a line from every sample to its centre, similar in logic to the plot(betadisper(...)) function in the R vegan package. Shaded convex hulls outline each group.

The plot does not run any permutation test itself. Run permanova and betadisper once and pass their results: the plot then draws the ordination from the betadisper result and annotates the figure with both tests, so the numbers on the figure are the same ones you report. Without results, the ordination is computed without a test and no annotation is added.

Centres are computed in the full PCoA space, as in the dispersion test, and then projected onto the plotted axes.

docs.text:
centroids(
    pm,
    column,
    components=(1, 2),
    hull=True,
    betadisper_result=None,
    permanova_result=None,
    type=None,

Plot samples and their group centres in PCoA space, like plot(vegan::betadisper(...)).

Each sample is joined to its group's centre by a line ("spider"), so both the separation between groups (centre positions) and the spread within groups (line lengths) are visible. Sample coordinates and centres come from pavvis.stats.permanova.betadisper, so the plot shows exactly what the dispersion test measured. Centres are computed in the full PCoA space and projected onto the two plotted axes, so a centre need not sit in the visual middle of its points.

The plot does not run any permutation test. Pass the results of pavvis.stats.permanova.betadisper and pavvis.stats.permanova.permanova to reuse their ordination and annotate the plot with their statistics, so the figure shows exactly the numbers reported elsewhere.

Clicking a group in the legend toggles its points, lines, centre and hull together. Groups are coloured in sorted order; colours repeat after eight groups.

None permanova_result DataFrame | None

The table returned by permanova(pm, column, ...). If given, its R², F and p are added to the annotation.

None type Literal['median', 'centroid'] | None

Group centre: 'median' (spatial median, vegan's default) or 'centroid' (mean). Defaults to the type of betadisper_result, or 'median' if none is given.

None

import pavvis.plots.pcoa as pcoa

Interpretation

Centres far apart with short spider lines indicate groups that differ in location. Long lines in one group and short lines in another indicate unequal dispersion, which the PERMDISP result in the annotation tests formally.

docs.title: Gene Presence
docs.text: This submodule contains plotting functions for visualising gene presence frequency across samples and per-sample gene counts across the PAV matrix. Assessment of gene presence can help to identify outlier samples and provide insights into the distribution of gene content across the dataset in relation to sample metadata.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The frequency of presence for a single gene can be calculated using the following calculation:

\[ \text{presence frequency} = \frac{\text{number of samples where gene} = 1}{\text{total number of samples}} \]

The result is a value in the range [0, 1], where 0 indicates a gene is absent in all samples and 1 means it is present in every sample.

After presence frequency has been calculated for each gene in the PAV matrix, a histogram can be plotted to summarise the distribution of presence across all genes, the larger the number of histogram bins, the larger the resolution available in the final plot.

This plot can be useful as a first-pass overview of the PAV matrix — a heavily left-skewed distribution indicates most genes are rare across the sample set. A heavily right-skewed distribution indicates most genes are present in the majority of samples.

docs.text:
from pavvis import PavMatrix
import pavvis.plots.presence as presence

pm = PavMatrix(
    matrix_path="path/to/pav.csv",
    metadata_path="path/to/metadata.csv",
)

presence.frequency_histogram(pm).show()

Interpretation

In the above plot, we see a right-skewed distribution of presence frequencies. This indicates that most genes in this PAV matrix are rare across the sample set — the majority of genes are only present in a few samples. It also confirms that there are very few core genes in this PAV matrix, which we could also assess using the class attribute pm.core_genes.

docs.title: Description

The number of present genes may differ according to sample metadata. A box-plot is a good way to represent the spread of present genes across all samples for a given metadata column. For each sample, the total number of present genes is calculated, and box plots are generated across each group in the metadata column. This plot can be useful for assessing the occurrence of batch effects and identifying groups of samples that may contain relatively diverse gene content.

Restriction on column type

This plot will only work if the metadata column is a discrete variable. To visualise relationships between total gene presence and continuous variables, see the scatter plot function below.

docs.title: UMAP plots
docs.text:
This submodule contains functions for visualising the UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) embedding of PAV matrices computed by pm.compute_umap(). UMAP reduces the high-dimensional PAV matrix — where each gene is a binary dimension — to two or three components, allowing the relationships between samples to be explored visually based on similarity in gene presence profiles.

UMAP plots can provide the first sign of relationships in the PAV matrix across sample metadata groups, as each point on the umap can be coloured according to both discrete or continuous metadata values. UMAP analysis does not provide a statistical framework for making conclusions, but can be very informative in deciding future directions of research based on the associations between metadata and the PAV matrix.

Prerequisites

You must call pm.compute_umap() before using any function documented on this page. See the PavMatrix API for details on available parameters such as n_neighbors, min_dist, and metric. This is a computationally intensive function for large PAV matrices, but the resultant embeddings are cached to allow for quick rebuilding of UMAP plots once the embeddings have been generated.

docs.text: Plots the first two UMAP components as a 2D scatter plot. Each point represents a sample. Points can be coloured by any metadata column — discrete columns produce a categorical legend; continuous columns use a Viridis colorscale. Clusters of samples in 2D space indicate groups with similar PAV profiles.

Interpretation

Tight, well-separated clusters suggest that groups differ substantially in their PAV profiles. Overlapping clusters indicate more similarity between groups. Points sitting far from any cluster may represent samples with unusual gene content worth investigating further. In the example plot, we see a small modern cluster far away from all other samples. Further analysis on this cluster revealed that these samples all contained an identical genomic introgression causing ~400 genes to be flagged as present across these samples, absent in the rest of the sample set.

docs.text:
Plots all three UMAP components as an interactive 3D scatter plot. Click and drag to rotate. Colouring behaves identically to scatter(). The third dimension can reveal additional structure collapsed in the 2D projection, particularly useful for datasets with complex population stratification and large number of samples.

Passing depth=True scales each point's size by its UMAP3 (z) coordinate, so points at higher z values appear larger. This provides a visual depth cue that makes it easier to read the z-axis when viewing the plot from a fixed angle, without needing to rotate to a favourable orientation.

Using depth scaling

depth=True is most effective when the default viewing angle places the z-axis running front-to-back. If the depth cue appears inverted, rotate the plot so that larger points are in the foreground.

docs.title: Variable gene plots
docs.text: This submodule contains plotting functions for visualising and exploring the variable gene pool within a PAV matrix. Variable genes — those present in at least one but not all samples — are often the most biologically informative component of a pangenome. These plots help characterise the distribution and exclusivity of variable gene content across groups defined in a metadata.csv file.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The frequency of presence for a single gene can be calculated using the following calculation:

\[ \text{presence frequency} = \frac{\text{number of samples where gene} = 1}{\text{total number of samples}} \]

The result is a value in the range [0, 1], where 0 indicates a gene is absent in all samples and 1 means it is present in every sample. After presence frequency has been calculated for each gene, a histogram can be plotted to summarise the distribution of presence across all genes.

Unlike the presence frequency histogram in the presence submodule, this plot colours each bin by gene category — absent, private, dispensable, soft core, and core — so the composition of each frequency range is visible at a glance.

This plot can be useful as a first-pass overview of the variable gene pool — a heavily left-skewed distribution indicates most variable genes are rare across the sample set, which is typical of an open pangenome. A distribution concentrated at higher frequencies suggests a more closed pangenome where most variable genes are shared broadly across the sample set.

The stacked colouring reveals the category composition at each frequency bin. A dominant private (low-frequency) bar suggests the pangenome is open and highly variable. A dominant soft-core or core bar at high frequencies suggests a more closed pangenome where most genes are conserved across samples.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
An exclusive gene is a variable gene present in at least one sample within a group and absent from every sample outside that group. Plotting exclusive gene counts per group allows the researcher to identify which groups harbour gene content that is not shared with any other group in the dataset.

A high exclusive gene count within a group may indicate lineage-specific content, such as adaptation to a local environment, unique metabolic capabilities, or a functional repertoire distinct from the rest of the sample set. Conversely, groups with very few exclusive genes may be more genomically similar to the broader population or may have fewer samples represented.

docs.title: Indicator genes
docs.text:
This submodule finds genes whose presence is characteristic of one group of samples, using the indicator value (IndVal) of Dufrêne & Legendre (1997) in its group-size-equalised form, IndVal.g. It is the PAV equivalent of indicspecies::multipatt(func="IndVal.g", duleg=TRUE) in R.

For a gene and a group, two components are combined:

  • A (specificity): how concentrated the gene is in the group. It is the gene's presence frequency in the group divided by the sum of its frequencies across all groups, so unequal group sizes do not bias it.
  • B (fidelity): the fraction of the group's samples that carry the gene.

The statistic is \(\sqrt{A \cdot B}\), between 0 and 1. A value of 1 means the gene is present in every sample of the group and absent from every other group. Each gene is assigned to the group where its value is highest, and a permutation test asks whether that value is larger than expected if group labels were random.

docs.title: indicator_genes
docs.text:
indicator_genes(pm, column, genes=None, permutations=999, random_state=None)

Indicator gene analysis (IndVal.g) for the groups of a discrete metadata column.

For each gene and group, specificity A is the gene's mean presence in the group divided by the sum of its mean presence across all groups (group-size equalised), and fidelity B is the fraction of the group's samples carrying the gene. The indicator value is sqrt(A·B), on the same [0, 1] scale as indicspecies::multipatt(func="IndVal.g", duleg=TRUE). Each gene is assigned to the group with the highest value.

Significance comes from permuting sample labels: p is the fraction of permutations where a gene's best-group value is at least as large as observed, with the observed value counted once. q-values use the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure over the tested genes only.

Scope: single groups only (no group combinations, unlike multipatt's default), and labels are permuted freely across all samples (no strata or blocks), so it is not suitable for nested designs. When two groups have exactly the same value, the first group in sorted order is reported; indicspecies picks one at random. Validated against indicspecies 1.8.0: statistic, A and B match to floating-point precision, and p-values agree within Monte Carlo error.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default pm PavMatrix

A PavMatrix instance.

required column str

A discrete metadata column defining the groups.

required genes list[str] | None

Gene IDs to test. Defaults to None (all variable genes). Core and absent genes cannot be indicators, so including them only weakens the multiple-testing correction.

None permutations int

Number of label permutations. Defaults to 999.

999 random_state int | None

Random seed for reproducibility. Defaults to None.

None

DataFrame indexed by gene ID with columns group, A, B, stat,

DataFrame

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from pavvis import PavMatrix
from pavvis.stats.indicator import indicator_genes

pm = PavMatrix("path/to/pav.csv", "path/to/metadata.csv")

res = indicator_genes(pm, "clade", permutations=9999, random_state=42)

sig = res[res.q_value < 0.05]
sig.groupby("group").size()                 # number of indicator genes per clade
sig[sig.group == "Modern"].head(20)         # strongest Modern indicators
res.join(pm.gene_table(column="clade"))     # add per-group presence counts

To plot the top indicator genes of each clade, pass res to plots.indicator.heatmap.

Interpretation

A high stat with high B but moderate A describes a gene common in the group that also occurs elsewhere. A high A with low B describes a gene that is rare but almost restricted to the group. With 999 permutations the smallest possible p-value is 0.001, which limits how many genes can pass a strict FDR threshold in a large matrix. Use more permutations when testing tens of thousands of genes.

Which genes are tested

By default only variable genes are tested. Core and absent genes cannot be indicators, and including them only weakens the multiple-testing correction.

docs.title: PERMANOVA and dispersion
docs.text:
This submodule tests whether groups of samples differ in gene content, using Jaccard distance (1 − Jaccard similarity, which ignores shared absences). The two functions are the PAV equivalents of vegan::adonis2 and vegan::betadisper with vegan::permutest.

PERMANOVA asks whether group centroids differ more than expected by chance. It is also sensitive to differences in spread, so a significant PERMANOVA should be read together with the dispersion test: if dispersions differ, the PERMANOVA result may reflect spread rather than location.

To show both on one figure, pass the results to pcoa.centroids:

import pavvis.plots.pcoa as pcoa

pcoa.centroids(pm, "clade", betadisper_result=bd, permanova_result=pa)

The plot reuses the results rather than re-running the tests, so the figure annotation matches the reported values.

docs.title: permanova
docs.text:
permanova(pm, column, permutations=999, random_state=None)

Equivalent to vegan::adonis2(dist ~ group, permutations=...) with Jaccard distance (1 − Jaccard similarity, from pm.compute_jaccard()). The pseudo-F is the ratio of between-group to within-group sums of squared distances, each divided by its degrees of freedom. Significance comes from permuting sample labels: p is the fraction of permutations with a pseudo-F at least as large as observed, with the observed value counted once.

PERMANOVA is sensitive to differences in dispersion as well as location. Check betadisper before interpreting a significant result as a shift in centroids.

R2 is the fraction of the total variation in Jaccard distance explained by the grouping. In the example, clade explains 8.6% of the variation in gene content. Small R² values are typical for PAV data, because much of the variable gene content differs between individual accessions.

docs.title: betadisper
docs.text:
betadisper(pm, column, type='median', permutations=999, random_state=None)

Multivariate homogeneity of group dispersions (PERMDISP) on Jaccard distance.

Follows vegan::betadisper and vegan::permutest. Samples are placed in PCoA space using all axes, including those with negative eigenvalues (Jaccard distance is not Euclidean). Each group's centre is computed separately in the positive and negative axis spaces, and a sample's distance to its group centre is z = sqrt(d₊² − d₋²), with negative values of d₊² − d₋² set to zero as in vegan. Dispersions are compared with a one-way ANOVA F on z; significance comes from refitting the ANOVA to permuted residuals (z minus its group mean), keeping the group centres fixed.

Validated against vegan 2.7.5 on the Amborella PAV data: distances and F match to floating-point precision with type='centroid'. With type='median', distances differ by ~1e-5 because vegan stops its BFGS search for the spatial median earlier than the Weiszfeld iteration used here.

A significant result means the groups differ in spread. In that case a significant PERMANOVA cannot be read purely as a difference in location.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default pm PavMatrix

A PavMatrix instance.

required column str

A discrete metadata column defining the groups.

required type Literal['median', 'centroid']

Group centre to measure distances from: 'median' (spatial median, vegan's default) or 'centroid' (mean). Defaults to 'median'.

'median' permutations int

Number of residual permutations. Defaults to 999.

999 random_state int | None

Random seed for reproducibility. Defaults to None.

None

Returns:

Type Description dict

Dict with keys:

dict
  • distances: pd.Series of distance to group centre, indexed by sample.
dict
  • centroids: DataFrame of group centres (groups × PCo1…) on the positive PCoA axes, matching pm.compute_pcoa(n_components=None).
dict
  • coordinates: DataFrame of sample coordinates on the same positive axes.
dict
  • explained: pd.Series of the fraction of positive-eigenvalue variation each axis explains.
dict
  • F: observed F statistic.
dict
  • p_value: permutation p-value.
dict
  • column, type, permutations: the arguments used.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If column is not a discrete metadata column or has fewer than 2 groups, or if type is not 'median' or 'centroid'.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from pavvis.stats.permanova import betadisper

bd = betadisper(pm, "clade", permutations=9999, random_state=42)
bd["F"], bd["p_value"]
bd["distances"].groupby(pm.metadata["clade"]).mean()   # mean distance to centre per clade

Interpretation

A significant result means some groups are more variable in gene content than others. Use pcoa.dispersion_boxplot(pm, "clade", betadisper_result=bd) to see which.
